claim: Three exported functions across two modules are capabilities the `@akasha/page-service` migration cut away and left as tombstones: a body of one `throw` under a declared return type that promises a value. `loadSave` says `Promise<IdleSave | null>` and returns nothing, ever. A `throw` body inhabits every return type, so nothing typechecks this and nothing ever will. This shape killed ten `akasha inference` commands on 2026-09-12, every one of which compiled: `landRow` was reached as effectively the first statement of `recordInferenceRun`, and it was mended at `4b1b844902b`. All three are the idle and gacha arm, live behind a web route rather than a command. Each says the page type it names is unheld, and both types are held, so the prose is wrong about why. Six more were removed rather than repaired. A check for this shape was measured against the whole tree and judged not to earn its place.

evidence:
The three still there, by path, name and declared return type. `alan/web/.server/idle-saves/idle-saves.module.code.ts:5` `loadSave` returns `Promise<IdleSave | null>`; `:9` `upsertSave` returns `Promise<void>`. `alan/web/.server/gacha-draw-context/gacha-draw-context.module.code.ts:9` `resolveDrawContext` returns `Promise<ResolvedDrawContext>`. Each message names what was taken away rather than what is unbuilt, so these are tombstones for capabilities that worked rather than stubs for capabilities not yet written. Each is also wrong about why: it says the page type it names is unheld, and the index files both `idle-save` and `persona-cover-image`, with shapes of 7 and 11 keys. The store that was taken away stops these, not an unheld type.

Six were removed rather than repaired. `loadAllSaves` went from `idle-saves` and `projectUserCards` from `idle-card-projecting`, each named by nothing; the save route calls `reprojectUserCardsSafely`, which logs and captures rather than throwing. The other four went at `71f1d7eaf6a`, `4844ab11824` and `3d076b222d2`. `getFilePagesByRelation` went from `page/access/modules/file-relation`, and `getPagesByRelation`, whose whole body was a call to it, went from `get-by-relation`; the rest of it went at `70da4f8d04d`. Two live callers reached the throw. `use-descendant-pages` swallowed the rejected promise in a `.catch` and set no rows, so a descendant-spanning listing filtered by one containment filter read `No pages match the current filters`, as though the question had landed and come back empty; at `ac778a29cfb` the guard went, and at `3deee033f2e` one ask of its page type answers for every type beneath. `alan/atlas-web/routes/atlas-trip` awaited the throw in its loader, so `/trip/:tripParam` answered 500; at `3dc353f34dc` its loader asks `getPages` for the locations whose `collection` is the collection's slug and lists them as that trip's stops. `pin-time-color` went with the throw and stays gone.

`writeChapterCompletion` and `writeChapterPosition` went from `alan/library/reading/modules/offline-reading`. `offline-text-sync` called both and does live work besides, so its completion drain and its position up-sync went while its chapter down-sync stayed, along with the listener that keeps Alan's place on the device. Position reading is untouched: `readLocalPosition` still answers `configureLocalPositionReader` in both roots and `reader-page-source` still restores the place when a chapter reopens. `position-store.json` is now the one local file written and never sent up: the completion queue, read by nothing once the drain went, was given up rather than drained again, at `d26bea3e518` and after. Nothing wrote `chapters-cache.json` — the `writeDocumentsFile` callers were `content-pages-fs` and two stores in `offline-text` — so the private `readCacheIndex` always answered empty, and it went with `EMPTY_CACHE_INDEX`, `CacheIndexPersistedSchema`, `migrateCacheIndex`, `CachedChapter`, `upsertCachedChapter`, `markChapterCompletedLocally`, `offlineReadingList` and `OfflineChapterListItem`.

`loadSmsExternalIdentities` went from `alan/harness/sms-access/modules/sms-allowlist`, which nothing but its own test imported. The live inbound path never went through it: `alan-web-api-sms-webhook.route.code.ts:139` asks `@akasha/page-service` for the `relationship` pages itself and builds its identities with `projectSmsIdentities`, and `:168` records a discard by messaging the `alan` seat. So `sms-discard` went too, and `sms-access` itself went at `74819cfc373`, page type and all.

Reachability, and how it was taken. I built the transitive import closure over literal specifiers, including `import type` and literal `await import()`, resolving `akasha/...` against the repository root, from every `.ts` under a given entry folder. From the 880 files under `command/pages/` it reaches 3,259 files; from `alan/web/routes` it reaches 1,402. That closure missed the `atlas-trip` loader, because atlas is a router app of its own with a routes folder of its own: a second live caller of one tombstone sat outside the entry folder walked. It would also miss a dynamic `import()` whose specifier is computed, a defaulted seam or an injected dependency, and any entry that is not TypeScript.

The check that was considered and rejected. Parsing all 84,136 `.ts` and `.tsx` files with the TypeScript compiler API found 14 exported functions whose body is one `throw`, and 41 counting those not exported. Of the 14, three already declare `never` or `Promise<never>` and so tell the truth: `retry.module.test-fixtures.ts:240`, `oauth-effects.module.test-fixtures.ts:259`, and `cluster-fetch.module.code.ts:91`. Two more are fixtures typed by a function alias rather than an inline annotation.

Two things sink the check. A syntax rule cannot make the distinction its own case rests on: `syntax-rule.page-type.ts:64` and `:70` state that a rule is handed one file already parsed and reads no index of its own, so it has no import graph and would refuse a live route-reached tombstone and an orphan alike. And the exception is the wrong shape. The honest way to declare a deliberate sole-`throw` is to return `never` or `Promise<never>`, assignable to any return type. But `loadSave` is meant to return `Promise<IdleSave | null>` again once a store answers; annotating it `Promise<never>` is as false as the present state in the other direction, and breaks every call site by design.

What this informs rather than decides: whether the three still there come back, and in what order. A tombstone that throws is at least loud where it is reached, and a silent wrong answer would not be; the fault is that the loudness arrives at a person's request rather than at a typecheck, and that the type says a value is coming. The `.catch` in `use-descendant-pages` is the case where even that failed: it answered with nothing, and it carries the reason out now instead.
